transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-02 14:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Maya (Orion ML Lead), Tom (Orion CTO), Evan (Orion Infra), Rina (Orion Security)

Summary: quick triage on throughput bottlenecks observed in Orion's on-prem pilot; focus on kernel selection, CUDA graph stability, KV cache behavior under bursty traffic, and quantized path regressions. Plan is to run targeted micro-benchmarks and then a short on-prem pilot with NVTX traces and packetized request streams.

Topics: kernel path selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM behavior, CUDA graph replay mismatches, persistent KV cache eviction, batching heuristics, quantization precision impact, VPC/on-prem constraints, SOC2/KMS notes.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick context — we heard the pilot saw tail latency spikes when you enabled persistent K V cache and mixed batch sizes. want to walk through what we saw and pair on microbenching.
[00:18] Maya (Orion): yep that matches. after about 20 minutes of steady traffic the 95th jumped from ~75ms to ~300ms. the median stayed low but the tail is the killer for our realtime triage.
[00:30] Priya (Redwood SE): ok, so two buckets usually: kernel-switching on the GPU side when sequence lengths vary, and eviction / cache churn in the K V cache leading to extra recompute. curious which model variant you're running?
[00:42] Evan (Orion): we're on a quantized 7B fp4-ish variant via TensorRT-LLM container, with a fallback to a v L L M python runtime for some older ops. the mix is... messy.
[00:56] Daniel Park (Redwood SE): that mix is a common source. TRT-LLM schedules a different kernel set and uses cuda-graph replay heavily; vllm's dynamic execution path avoids some of that but has different memory layout, so warmups can be inconsistent.
[01:10] Tom (CTO): can you unpack the cuda-graph bit — we saw occasional replay mismatches where replay seemed to succeed but perf dropped after a few minutes.
[01:20] Priya: yeah, so cuda-graph replay is deterministic replay of a launch sequence. but in practice when you have conditional code paths (like kv cache hits vs misses) the replay path can be stale — leading to kernel mismatch and falling back to a slower execution schedule and sometimes extra memcpy. also nvlink fragmentation matters on multi-gpu.
[01:45] Maya: fragmentation? like NV link bandwidth flapping? we do have 2 x A100s in a DGX rack and sometimes the node switches to single-GPU paths during heavy IO.
[01:56] Daniel: hmm that could be either p2p path fallback or a driver scheduler issue. we've seen cases where a bad cuda-graph capture captured a kernel set that assumed certain nvlink peer array layout; when the runtime chooses a different interconnect, the graph can't be used efficiently and you see perf regressions.
[02:15] Evan: on our side we also saw more GPU kernels scheduled at the same time — occupancy dropped because of mixed precision kernels getting different launch configs.
[02:27] Priya: right. quantization changes can alter launch tiling and occupancy, so a 4-bit path vs 8-bit or fp16 can pick different kernels (tensor cores vs fallback). that explains some of your fluctuating throughput.
[02:40] Maya: what about KV cache eviction — why would that spike spikes?
[02:45] Priya: when KV cache is persistent and you get concurrent requests with different prefixes, eviction policy can cause thrashing. for example if one tenant's long prefix keeps being reinserted, it evicts other hot prefixes and forces more KV materialize work. the runtime may switch to a kernel path that recomputes keys instead of using cached k/v tensors.
[03:07] Tom: ok so behaviour is multi-factor. do you have a suggested triage checklist?
[03:12] Alex: yeah quick checklist: 1) capture NVTX traces over a 10m window capturing both good and bad periods; 2) run micro-benchmarks that sweep batch sizes and sequence lengths on TRT-LLM and vllm separately; 3) check kernel launch counts and occupancy; 4) run a synthetic burst test to exercise eviction pressure; 5) validate cuda-graph capture/replay stable across our driver version.
[03:40] Maya: NVTX sample — can you give us an example? we tried once but the traces were noisy.
[03:45] Priya: we'll share a small script that toggles prefixes, adds jitter, and annotates nvtx at each launcher. it's in the micro-bench repo. i'll also include an example of a cuda-graph capture mismatch pattern.
[03:59] Evan: about batching heuristics — our traffic is bursty. sometimes we want very low latency single-stream requests, sometimes large batched requests. how does Redwood handle mixed workloads?
[04:10] Daniel: the runtime has per-route policies: you can reserve a low-latency lane with small batching and a throughput lane with larger aggregation. the scheduler can route by token budget or deadline. that said, on a single machine the KV cache and kernel choice are global resources, so if the throughput lane causes eviction it can still impact the latency lane.
[04:34] Tom: so isolation is imperfect on shared private clusters. what about dedicated capacity?
[04:38] Alex: Dedicated capacity gives you isolated GPU pools which reduces noisy neighbor effects, and we can pin model variants and kernel sets per pool. it's not free — but for tight SLOs it often pays off.
[04:50] Maya: pricing aside, we'd like to try a short on-prem run with full telemetry. expected steps?
[04:55] Alex: we suggest a 2-3 day slot where we reproduce your workload, run the micro-bench scripts, and iterate on kernel flags and capture traces. Priya will drive the benching.
[05:07] Rina (Security): quick security note — we need to validate KMS usage, audit logs, and SOC2 alignment if any logs leave our VPC. on-prem will be easier but we need a paper trail.
[05:19] Priya: noted — we can share our SOC2 summary and the KMS integration guide. for on-prem we support customer-managed H S M and KM S providers.
[05:28] Evan: earlier you mentioned a v L L M fallback for some ops — what are typical op mismatches?
[05:33] Daniel: vllm often uses a fused attention kernel for certain sequence lengths; TRT-LLM may not have that fusion and instead uses a different tiling. edge ops like rotary embeddings or some custom position encodings sometimes fall back to the python forward which kills throughput.
[05:49] Maya: any quick heuristics to detect whether our bottleneck is kernel selection vs KV thrashing?
[05:54] Priya: yes — kernel selection issues usually show up as changes in kernel names and launch parameters in nvprof/nvtx traces and occupancy shifts. KV thrashing shows as repeated memory transfers labeled K V materialize or repeated scatter/gather patterns, and latency correlates with host<->device memcpy spikes.
[06:13] Tom: can we get concrete numbers? in our run the 99th went to 520ms. what's a typical baseline we should compare to for a 7B quantized model?
[06:22] Alex: ballpark for a well-tuned TRT-LLM path on an A100, single-token latency with small batch might be 30–60ms depending on sequence length; throughput lane with batching could hit several hundred tokens/sec. if you're seeing 500ms 99th that's indicative of replay fallback, eviction recompute, or driver throttling.
[06:42] Evan: we also saw increased CPU utilization on the host when the tail hit.
[06:46] Daniel: yep that ties to extra memcpy and scheduling overhead; when the GPU kernel path doesn't match the capture, the CPU often takes over more orchestration, increasing host CPU.
[06:56] Priya: for quantization regression: if you move from fp16 to 4-bit, some ops may lose tensor core support and fall back to more general kernels. that increases latency per-token but reduces memory footprint. it's a trade off.
[07:14] Maya: could quantization amplify eviction because model tensors shrink and we fit more in cache so eviction policy flips?
[07:21] Priya: interesting point — yes, lower precision changes memory pressure and can change eviction patterns; sometimes it actually reduces eviction because more fits; other times it increases ephemeral allocations for quant-dequant paths causing churn. it's model and implementation dependent.
[07:39] Alex: next step practical plan: run two isolated micro-bench runs — TRT-LLM only, vllm only — with the same request distribution and NVTX. then a mixed-run to reproduce your production mix. we'll compare kernel launch histograms, memcpy counters, and cuda-graph replay success rates.
[07:56] Maya: timeline?
[07:58] Alex: we can ship the bench script today, Priya will run the first sweep Thursday, then we reconvene Friday for initial findings and scheduling the 2-day on-prem slot next week.
[08:10] Rina: also add a short checklist for data exfil concerns; we'll need to review the audit logs and encryption in transit at the start.
[08:18] Alex: yes, we'll include the compliance checklist.
[08:22] Evan: any known driver versions that are problematic for cuda-graph?
[08:26] Daniel: older 470-5xx driver sets had more graph instability; we recommend a recent 520+ driver and matching CUDA runtime. we'll include a recommended matrix.
[08:38] Priya: one more debugging tip: enable per-kernel timing and NOT collapse names in NVTX so you can see kernel aliasing. sometimes different kernels have very similar names and get aggregated in tooling which hides the pattern.
[08:52] Maya: good call.
[08:54] Tom: what about model rollout strategies — can we A/B test a quantized variant safely?
[08:59] Alex: yes, Redwood supports canary rollouts with automatic fallback. you can route a small percentage of requests to quant path and monitor quality and latency; if quality drops we automatically fallback to the non-quant path.
[09:12] Maya: quality monitoring — we have a small prompt-set; can you hook that into the trial?
[09:16] Priya: absolutely, we'll add your eval prompts to the quality monitor and wire alerts for perplexity/response diff thresholds.
[09:23] Evan: circling back — is there an easy way to detect cuda-graph fallback in prod without NVTX? we don't want NVTX overhead in prod.
[09:31] Daniel: yes you can sample telemetry counters exposed by the runtime — graph replay success rates, fallback counts, kernel mismatch counts. low-overhead sampling once a minute is reasonable and we can correlate with latency spikes.
[09:45] Maya: great. let's talk about the pilot node requirements — what do you need from our side for the 2-day run?
[09:50] Priya: 1) root level nvprof/nvtx access or equivalent user perms, 2) the same driver/CUDA we use in the recommended matrix, 3) representative dataset (sample traffic), 4) brief network diagram showing NVLink/PCIe layout.
[10:07] Evan: we can prepare that. do you need HSM access?
[10:10] Alex: only if we need to test KMS integration. for the bench it's optional.
[10:14] Rina: we'll schedule a separate security session if you need access to keys.
[10:19] Maya: ok last set of questions — how much does host memory fragmentation influence KV eviction?
[10:25] Priya: host memory fragmentation can cause page-pinning failures which increases memcpy latency; also if you use unified virtual addressing with pinned pages, fragmentation reduces effective contiguous allocations causing more host paging. it's less common but shows up especially on long-lived processes with variable allocations.
[10:43] Tom: any gotchas with our cloud provider on-prem interconnect? we use a colo with shared switch fabric.
[10:49] Daniel: shared fabric can add jitter; NVLink ensures peer-to-peer but once you cross node boundaries or use RoCE the effective latency increases; in that case we recommend keeping latency-sensitive lanes on the same physical machine or using Dedicated Capacity.
[11:05] Alex: wrapping up — action items (recap): Priya share micro-bench + nvtx examples; Alex share Dedicated pricing and compliance docs; Maya/Evan schedule 2-day on-prem window and provide driver/CUDA + network diagram; Redwood to produce recommended driver matrix and initial bench results by Friday.
[11:28] Maya: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[11:30] Tom: thanks.
[11:32] Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links.

References shared: micro-bench repo (link), NVTX trace example (link), Redwood SOC2 summary (link), Dedicated pricing deck (link).
